strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored question: which layers are most useful for influence estimation in LLMs and how to aggregate layer-wise influence scores.

Conducts a broad empirical study across four LLM families/scales (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE datasets, multiple influence methods (TracIn, Cosine, DataInf, WE variants), and 10 random seeds.
Challenges the influential claim from Yeh et al. (2022) that first/embedding layers are best, and provides empirical evidence that middle attention layers can be more effective in several settings.

Proposes Rank and Vote aggregation strategies for combining influence scores across layers and validation samples; Vote improves over mean aggregation for TracIn and DataInf on several models and tasks.
Introduces Noise Detection Rate (NDR) and NDR-AUC as proxy metrics and shows moderate-to-strong correlations with downstream accuracy after filtering in some settings.

Provides a theoretical counterexample suggesting that high-cancellation weights can, in principle, improve influence-based separation, which motivates a re-examination of the cancellation-effect assumption.
Includes extensive appendices with layer rankings, per-dataset accuracies, noise distributions, and aggregation comparisons, which gives useful transparency into the empirical behavior.

The practical motivation is clear: reducing the cost of influence estimation by selecting informative layers and improving aggregation could make influence functions more usable for LLM data auditing.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak and not rigorously established. The proof of Theorem 5.1 relies on informal gradient-cancellation arguments, unjustified inequalities, and a hand-wavy contradiction ('universal anti-alignment is impossible'); it does not rigorously show that the cancellation effect is unreliable in general.

The central empirical claim that middle attention layers are better is not consistent across models: RoBERTa peaks in later attention layers, Llama methods often fail to beat Random, Qwen favors middle layers, and Mistral favors early/middle layers. The paper sometimes overstates a general conclusion from mixed evidence.

The proposed NDR and AUC metrics require ground-truth noise labels, which are unavailable in real-world influence auditing. This substantially limits their practical utility as 'external' proxies for downstream performance.

The evaluation is narrow relative to LLM influence estimation: it uses GLUE classification tasks, synthetic label noise, small subsets (e.g., 4500 training samples), LoRA fine-tuning, and a classification head. It does not evaluate generative LLM attribution, real noisy data, pretraining, or full fine-tuning, so generalization to actual LLM data influence is uncertain.

The cancellation metric is not computed as in the original Yeh et al. formulation: it is estimated on a single checkpoint in evaluation mode rather than accumulated over size-one training batches. This may make the comparison with prior work less direct and could affect the conclusions.

Aggregation methods Rank and Vote are simple heuristics, not deeply novel, and their benefits are inconsistent: Vote often helps TracIn/DataInf but can degrade Cosine, and Rank is usually weaker. There is little theoretical motivation for when these methods should be preferred.

The paper lacks important baselines: no comparison to other layer-selection criteria, no comparison to alternative label-noise detection methods, and no comparison to more sophisticated aggregation/ensemble schemes.

Statistical rigor is limited: 10 runs with Wilcoxon tests at p < 0.1 and a 1% mean-change threshold are relatively weak, especially given the noisy GLUE accuracies and the many configurations compared.

For Llama-3.2 1B, influence-based filtering often does not outperform the Random baseline. This undermines the claim that the proposed layer/aggregation choices provide a robust practical improvement.

Reproducibility is unclear: there is no statement about code, data, or model checkpoint release. Hyperparameters are mostly in the appendix, but the exact implementation details needed to reproduce influence computations and aggregation are incomplete.

The paper is difficult to read in places: notation is inconsistent (e.g., x vs.  ar{x}, l vs.  ar{l}), equations are sometimes undefined or poorly explained, and the connection between theoretical claims and experimental protocol is not always clear.

The positioning is somewhat incremental: it is primarily an empirical critique of prior work plus simple aggregation heuristics and intuitive proxy metrics. For a top-tier AI venue, the contribution may be insufficient without stronger theory, a new influence method, or broader evidence.

strengths: Broad empirical study spanning multiple LLMs, GLUE datasets, influence methods, layer groups, and aggregation strategies, with 10 seeds per configuration.
Addresses a relevant and practically important problem: how to choose layers and aggregate influence scores for LLM data attribution.
Proposes Rank and Vote aggregation methods and shows some improvements over mean aggregation for TracIn and DataInf on certain models/tasks.
Attempts to challenge the prior cancellation-effect assumption with empirical correlations and a theoretical counterexample.
Provides extensive appendices with layer rankings, noise distributions, accuracy trends, and experimental setup details.
weaknesses: The central claim that middle attention layers are better is not consistently supported. Results vary by model: Llama influence methods fail to beat Random, RoBERTa peaks in later layers, Mistral TracIn peaks in early layers, and Qwen is often discussed but omitted from key tables. The title and abstract overstate the findings.

Theorem 5.1 is not rigorous. The proof is handwavy, relies on an unclear contradiction and a vague impossibility argument, and only shows existence of one validation point where including a high-cancellation weight can improve separation between two samples. It does not establish that the cancellation effect is generally unreliable or that middle layers are better.

Evaluation likely leaks test information: reporting best test-set accuracy after retraining suggests model selection on the test set, which invalidates the main performance comparisons. Validation-based selection is needed.

The experimental setting uses very small GLUE subsets and LoRA-only fine-tuning with compressed embeddings. Conclusions about LLM layer influence may not generalize to full fine-tuning or standard influence estimation, and the comparison to Yeh et al. is not apples-to-apples.

NDR and AUC require ground-truth noise labels, so they are not practical proxies for real unlabeled auditing without retraining. NDR is essentially standard noise recall, and the reported correlations are only moderate (often 0.5-0.7) with many non-significant cases, contradicting claims of strong predictive capability.

Aggregation claims are overbroad. Vote degrades Cosine performance in Figure 3, yet the paper claims it consistently outperforms mean aggregation. Rank and Vote are standard ranking/voting ensembles with limited novelty and no theoretical justification.

Results are inconsistent and sometimes contradict the main narrative: Random can outperform influence methods on Llama, CL is sometimes better than claimed, and Vote can hurt on CoLA/QQP. The layer rankings vary substantially by model, method, and task.

Missing or weak baselines: no full-gradient influence baseline, no random-layer-selection baseline, no comparison to other layer-selection heuristics, and no ablation on filtering percentage beyond 30%.

The layer-choice analysis is confounded by LoRA modules: influence is computed on LoRA parameters in query/value projections and the classification head, while embeddings are frozen. Conclusions about original model layers are therefore questionable.
Statistical methodology is weak: Wilcoxon tests at p < 0.1 with 10 seeds and no multiple-comparison correction. Many significance claims are likely underpowered or false positives.

Clarity and positioning are problematic. The title 'First is Not Really Better Than Last' is misleading because the paper actually finds last/CL generally worst. The definition of 'middle' shifts across models, and the contribution is incremental relative to prior influence-function and layer-selection work.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release, incomplete hyperparameters, confusing DataInf notation, garbled appendix references/figures, and missing Qwen results in Table 2 despite claiming Qwen experiments.
The paper lacks discussion of limitations, computational cost, real-world applicability, and potential negative uses, which is important for data auditing methods.

strengths: Broad empirical study across four LLMs (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B) and eight GLUE datasets, using multiple influence functions and 10 seeds, which strengthens the generality of the findings.

Challenges the prior cancellation-effect assumption from Yeh et al. (2022) with both empirical correlations and a theoretical counterexample, which is a useful contribution to the influence-estimation literature.
Proposes and evaluates practical alternatives to mean aggregation (Rank and Vote), showing that Vote often improves over averaging, especially for DataInf and TracIn on larger models.

Introduces NDR and AUC as proxy metrics for downstream influence performance, with moderate-to-strong correlations to post-filtering accuracy and potential to reduce costly retraining-based evaluation.
Provides actionable insights on layer choice, indicating that early/middle attention layers are often more informative than embedding or classification-head layers for larger LLMs.
The experimental protocol is relatively thorough, including checkpoint selection, noise injection, layer grouping, and extensive appendix material with additional rankings and noise distributions.
weaknesses: The theoretical result in Theorem 5.1 is not rigorously proved; the derivation uses handwavy steps, unjustified assumptions, and a questionable contradiction argument, so it does not convincingly establish the claimed counterexample.
The cancellation effect is measured at a single checkpoint in evaluation mode rather than over the training trajectory as originally formulated, which may not faithfully test Yeh et al.'s hypothesis.

The proposed aggregation methods are simple ranking/voting heuristics and are only compared against mean averaging; missing comparisons to other robust aggregation baselines (median, trimmed mean, consensus/sign agreement) and lacking theoretical justification.

Evaluation relies on synthetic label noise in GLUE benchmarks; real-world detrimental or mislabeled samples may have different structure, and for Llama the influence methods often fail to beat Random, weakening the generality of the conclusions.
NDR and AUC require ground-truth noise labels to compute, limiting their practical use as external evaluation proxies in real auditing scenarios where such labels are unavailable.

Layer grouping is coarse (groups of attention layers) and experiments use LoRA plus compressed embeddings, so it is unclear whether the layer-choice findings transfer to full fine-tuning or individual-layer influence estimation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as the general superiority of middle attention layers, given mixed model/task/method-dependent results and the fact that RoBERTa TracIn performs best on WE.
Reproducibility could be improved: no code/data release is mentioned, and the manuscript contains typos, citation-formatting issues, and dense figures/tables that make some results hard to parse.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: which layers and aggregation strategies are most effective for gradient-based influence estimation in LLMs, directly challenging a prior seminal conclusion by Yeh et al. (2022).

Provides a broad empirical study across four LLMs (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE tasks, multiple influence methods (TracIn, Cosine, DataInf), LoRA modules, 10 random seeds, and additional autoregressive datasets in the appendix.

Introduces simple but often effective aggregation alternatives, Rank and Vote, which can substantially improve filtering performance over standard mean aggregation, especially for TracIn and DataInf on Mistral 7B.

Proposes NDR and AUC as proxy metrics for downstream influence performance and shows moderate-to-strong correlations under Vote aggregation, suggesting a potentially useful direction for reducing retraining-based evaluation.
Offers practical recommendations, such as using LoRA Value B modules and early/middle attention layers, which could be useful for practitioners performing influence-based data auditing.
Includes extensive appendix material, statistical testing, and a reproducibility statement with code release, random seeds, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The central claim that middle attention layers are better estimators is not consistently supported: RoBERTa-Large performs best on later attention layers, Mistral 7B often prefers early/middle layers depending on method, and Llama-3.2 1B influence methods frequently fail to outperform the random filtering baseline. The paper overstates the generality of its layer-choice conclusion.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1 / G.1) is not rigorous. The proof relies on vague arguments such as 'universal anti-alignment is impossible' and does not clearly establish the result under the cancellation metric as defined. It is also limited to TracIn and does not obviously extend to the broader class of influence functions discussed.

The evaluation uses 'best test accuracy' after retraining, which can leak test information through epoch/model selection. A proper protocol should select checkpoints via validation performance and report test performance once. This issue may inflate or distort the reported comparisons.

The cancellation-effect computation differs from the original formulation of Yeh et al. (2022): it is measured on a single checkpoint in evaluation mode and aggregated over layer groups, so the empirical refutation may not be a direct test of the original cancellation hypothesis.

The proposed aggregation methods are simple heuristics and are only compared against mean aggregation. There is no comparison to other robust aggregation baselines such as median, trimmed mean, or established rank-aggregation methods, and Vote's hyperparameter k lacks principled selection.

NDR and AUC require ground-truth knowledge of which training samples are noisy. This limits their usefulness as external proxy metrics for real-world unlabeled datasets, where the noise labels are unavailable.

Some experimental conclusions rely on pairwise win rates, arbitrary thresholds, and multiple comparisons over many configurations. Statistical significance and practical significance are not always clearly separated, and the small test sets (500 samples) increase variance.

Clarity and presentation could be improved: there are typographical errors (e.g., 'fracIn', 'Dutaluf', 'bettser'), dense figures/tables, and some methodological details, such as final checkpoint selection for retraining, are unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: layer selection and score aggregation for influence-function-based data attribution in LLMs.

Conducts a broad empirical study across several models (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), eight GLUE tasks, multiple influence methods (TracIn, Cosine, DataInf), and 10 random seeds.
Attempts to challenge the prior cancellation-effect hypothesis with both empirical correlation analysis and a theoretical counterexample.
Proposes aggregation strategies (Rank and Vote) that sometimes improve over standard mean aggregation, especially for Mistral 7B and DataInf/TracIn.
Introduces NDR/AUC diagnostic metrics and reports moderate-to-strong correlations with downstream filtering performance in some settings.
Provides a practical recommendation around LoRA Value B modules, which may be useful for practitioners using PEFT-based influence estimation.
Includes additional experiments on autoregressive datasets and several recent influence methods in the appendix.
Open-source code and reproducibility statement are mentioned, though the link is omitted in the manuscript.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weak and non-rigorous. The proof of Theorem 5.1 uses informal scalar-gradient assumptions, questionable inequalities, and an unproven claim that 'universal anti-alignment is impossible.' It only shows a possible counterexample, not that the cancellation effect is generally unreliable.

The empirical evaluation selects the 'best test accuracy' after retraining, which leaks the test set into model/checkpoint selection. This biases comparisons and undermines the reliability of the main layer/aggregation conclusions.

NDR and AUC require ground-truth noise labels. They are therefore not practical external metrics for evaluating influence methods on real unlabeled data, contrary to the paper's framing. Correlations are also only moderate (0.5-0.7) and non-significant in several cases, especially for Llama-3.2 1B.

The central claim that middle attention layers are better is not consistently supported. Results vary by model: RoBERTa favors later attention layers, Llama configurations fail to beat Random, and Qwen/Mistral favor early-to-middle groups. The conclusion should be model/task/method-dependent rather than a general 'middle layers are better' claim.

The layer grouping is arbitrary (four equal attention groups), and conclusions about 'middle' layers depend heavily on these boundaries. Individual-layer behavior is not sufficiently analyzed in the main text.

The Rank and Vote equations are unclear and notationally inconsistent. In particular, k is described both as a number of votes and as a filtering percentage/threshold, making the Vote method difficult to reproduce and evaluate.

Novelty is limited: NDR/AUC are standard diagnostic metrics, and Rank/Vote are simple heuristic aggregations. The paper does not compare against other natural aggregation alternatives such as median, trimmed mean, sign voting, or Borda variants.

Missing strong baselines for label-noise detection and data filtering (e.g., loss, confidence, AUM, small-loss, or other data valuation methods). The only baselines are Random and an oracle Full setting.

The experimental setup uses small validation/test subsets (500 samples), synthetic binary label noise, and LoRA/embedding compression, which may not generalize to full fine-tuning or generative LLM tasks.

The comparison to Yeh et al. (2022) is not apples-to-apples: different models, tasks, noise injection, parameterization, and evaluation protocol. The paper therefore does not directly refute their findings, despite claiming to contradict prior knowledge.

The practical recommendation is confounded: the strongest results often come from LoRA Value B modules, so the benefit may be due to module type rather than 'middle layers.' The paper does not disentangle these factors.
Statistical analysis is weak: p<0.1 is used for significance, multiple comparisons are not corrected, and win-rate thresholds are not rigorously justified.

Presentation is poor: many typos and formatting issues (e.g., 'fracIn', 'Dutaluf', inconsistent model names), confusing tables/figures, undefined notation, and missing labels in Table 2 make the paper hard to follow and reproduce.

The paper overclaims relative to the evidence. For Llama-3.2 1B, influence methods fail to outperform Random, which directly undermines broad claims about better layer choices and aggregation strategies.
The code URL is missing from the reproducibility statement, and key implementation details (LoRA rank/alpha, exact noise injection, checkpoint selection) are incomplete.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: layer choice and score aggregation for influence estimation in LLMs, with practical implications for data auditing and training-data debugging.

Challenges prior work (Yeh et al., 2022) with a multi-model empirical study and a theoretical counterexample, providing concrete evidence that the cancellation effect is not a reliable predictor of layer usefulness.

Extensive experimental protocol: 4 LLMs (RoBERTa-Large, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B, Mistral 7B), 8 GLUE datasets, multiple influence methods (TracIn, Cosine, DataInf, WE variants), 10 seeds, pairwise win-rate comparisons, and statistical testing.

Proposes simple but effective aggregation strategies (Rank and Vote) that improve downstream accuracy in several configurations, especially Vote for Mistral/DataInf/TracIn, with substantial win-rate gains.

Introduces NDR/AUC proxy metrics that show moderate-to-strong correlations with downstream task accuracy, offering a way to reduce costly retraining when evaluating influence methods on benchmarks with known noise labels.
Good reproducibility: code is open-sourced, random seeds and hardware are specified, and the appendix provides detailed setup and additional results.
Provides practical recommendations (e.g., using LoRA Value B modules) and extends the analysis to autoregressive datasets and additional influence methods in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical proof of Theorem 5.1/G.1 is not rigorous: it relies on informal phrases such as 'typically' and an asserted impossibility of universal anti-alignment, rather than a formal proof. The theorem may only establish a narrow counterexample under strong assumptions.

The cancellation effect is computed at a single checkpoint in evaluation mode, rather than throughout fine-tuning as in Yeh et al. (2022). This may not faithfully test the original hypothesis and weakens the comparison to prior work.

Word embeddings are frozen during training, yet gradients are computed for influence estimation on WE. This raises concerns about whether WE influence scores are meaningful or comparable to prior work where embeddings are trained.

NDR and AUC require ground-truth noise labels, so they are not a general proxy for real-world unlabeled auditing. They are essentially noise-detection precision/AUC on synthetic benchmarks, which limits their claimed utility.

The layer-choice conclusions are model- and method-dependent: 'middle attention layers' are not universally best (e.g., RoBERTa often favors later layers, and Llama influence methods fail to beat random filtering). The abstract and title overstate the universality of the finding.

The evaluation uses relatively small subsets (up to 4500 training samples, 500 validation/test) and synthetic 20% label noise on GLUE. This may not reflect realistic LLM fine-tuning scales or natural noise distributions.
Aggregation comparison is limited to mean vs. Rank/Vote; there is no comparison to other robust aggregators (e.g., median, trimmed mean, max) or random layer selection baselines.
No runtime or computational-cost analysis is provided for the proposed aggregation methods, despite computational feasibility being a central motivation.
The proxy metrics are only correlated on the same set of configurations; no held-out evaluation demonstrates that NDR/AUC can predict downstream performance for unseen methods or models.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, e.g., 'better methods for evaluating influence score efficacy in LLMs without undertaking model retraining' when NDR still requires known mislabeled samples.
